documents.unit: Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Office of Undergraduate Education (Harvard College)
documents.title: Generative AI Guidance
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single rule; "All faculty are required to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use" and it offers sample policies from "maximally restrictive" to "fully-encouraging", leaving the choice to each course.
tiers: Maximally restrictive draft (no AI at any stage)
Mixed draft (disallowed unless stated per assignment)
documents.summary: The Harvard College OUE page requires each instructor to publish a generative-AI policy and supplies three sample policies. An FAQ discusses detectors, privacy and adapting teaching.

units.why: Mandatory language: "All faculty are required to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use". It binds instructors and concerns communicating expectations, so P09 (state AI expectations), not P04, because it does not itself leave the rule to instructors.
units.anchor: All faculty are required to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use

units.why: "you should post your policy on your Canvas site" tells instructors where to communicate their rule; a recommendation about communication, so P09.
units.anchor: you should post your policy on your Canvas site

units.why: "different classes at Harvard could implement different AI policies, and it is the student's responsibility to conform to expectations for each course" says one course's rule does not carry over; P11 fits better than P04 because the point is non-transfer for the student. The sentence repeats in all three samples and is coded once.
units.anchor: it is the student’s responsibility to conform to expectations for each course

units.why: Instructors may "choose from among the below example policies ... or design your own", so the decision sits with each instructor: P04, not P05, since the samples are drafts to adopt rather than defined tiers of use.
units.anchor: You can choose from among the below example policies to add to your Canvas site
units.frag_end: suit the needs of your course.

units.why: The page offers sample policies from "maximally restrictive" through "mixed" to "fully-encouraging"; a named range of options is P05 (explicit tiers), not P04, which is coded separately.
units.anchor: A maximally restrictive draft policy:
units.policy: Three draft policies are offered: maximally restrictive, fully-encouraging and mixed.

units.why: Restrictive sample: "We specifically forbid the use of ChatGPT or any other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools"; "at all stages ... including preliminary ones" makes it a default ban on the work, P01.
units.anchor: forbid the use of ChatGPT or any other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools

units.why: Restrictive sample: "all work students submit for this course will be their own". Submitted work must be the student's own, so P29.
units.anchor: all work students submit for this course will be their own

units.why: "we expect for the assignment to list all team members who participated" is a rule about naming collaborators on group work; no type covers crediting team members, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: we expect for the assignment to list all team members who participated
units.uncovered_note: Group assignments must list all participating team members (collaboration attribution, not AI-specific).

units.why: "Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct" classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct, P36. It repeats in all three samples and is coded once.
units.anchor: Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct.

units.why: Encouraging sample: "This course encourages students to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools ... for all assignments and assessments", a default of encouraged use, P02.
units.anchor: encourages students to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools

units.why: "Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" requires acknowledgement of AI use in the submission, P24.
units.anchor: Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited.

units.why: "It is each student's responsibility to assess the validity and applicability of any GAI output" makes students check AI output: P31 rather than P29 because the duty named is assessing validity. The "final responsibility" sentence is coded separately as P29.
units.anchor: assess the validity and applicability of any GAI output that is submitted

units.why: "you bear the final responsibility" says the student owns the AI output they submit, P29.
units.anchor: you bear the final responsibility

units.why: Mixed sample: "Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage the use of generative artificial intelligence" shows permission varies by assignment, P04.
units.anchor: Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage

units.why: "The default is that such use is disallowed unless otherwise stated" sets a ban with stated exceptions for the course. P01 chosen over P06 because it states the course default, not a rule for a silent syllabus.
units.anchor: The default is that such use is disallowed unless otherwise stated.

units.why: "Respondus, a new browser lockdown tool ... for in-person seated exams and quizzes to ensure that students do not use AI unless the course asks them to" offers closed-device exams, P22.
units.anchor: browser lockdown tool, on their Canvas site(s) to use for in-person seated exams and quizzes
units.frag_end: unless the course asks them to do so.

units.why: "It would be inadvisable to count on automated methods for GAI detection" advises against relying on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: It would be inadvisable to count on automated methods for GAI detection.

units.why: "FAS does not plan to provide/license such a tool" (an AI-use detector) says the institution will not supply detection; P39 since it concerns not relying on detectors.
units.anchor: FAS does not plan to provide/license such a tool for use in courses.

units.why: The FAQ says FAS "does not plan to provide/license" a tool that blocks internet access for laptop exams. This is an institutional choice about proctoring technology; P22 is the rule against AI on exams, which this is not, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: technologies for exam proctoring that aim to block students from using the internet
units.uncovered_note: FAS will not provide or license internet-blocking exam proctoring technology.

units.why: "No confidential information can be loaded into GAI systems, since there is no expectation of privacy" is a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: No confidential information can be loaded into GAI systems

units.why: "Faculty must get documented permission from students before putting original student content into any generative AI tool" limits instructor use of student work. P50 (protect personal data) chosen over P59 because the concern is privacy and consent.
units.anchor: Faculty must get documented permission from students before putting original student content

units.why: "students should be made aware of the risks of entering their original work into such tools" tells instructors to warn students of privacy risk, P50.
units.anchor: students should be made aware of the risks of entering their original work

units.why: "terms of service allow the company to access any information fed into it" states that the tool keeps submitted prompts, P50.
units.anchor: terms of service allow the company to access any information fed into it

units.why: "We should assume that all our students are proficient with these tools and should adjust our expectations accordingly" tells instructors to adapt to AI, P35.
units.anchor: should adjust our expectations accordingly

units.why: "A good first step is to feed representative assignments from your upcoming courses into a GAI tool" advises instructors to learn what AI does before setting policy: P63 rather than P35.
units.anchor: feed representative assignments from your upcoming courses into a GAI tool such as ChatGPT

units.why: "decide on and disseminate a course-by-course policy on student use of GAI tools" leaves the rule to each course: P04 over P09 since the emphasis is who decides.
units.anchor: decide on and disseminate a course-by-course policy on student use of GAI tools

units.why: "We also need to teach our students how to use these tools in an ethical and responsible manner" makes teaching responsible AI use a goal, P44.
units.anchor: teach our students how to use these tools in an ethical and responsible manner

units.why: "Harvard supports responsible experimentation with generative AI tools" with named considerations (security, privacy, copyright, integrity) is an institution-level principle, P56.
units.anchor: Harvard supports responsible experimentation with generative AI tools

units.why: "some of the material they provide as factual are incorrect" warns that AI output can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: some of the material they provide as factual are incorrect

units.why: "GAI responses will reflect the biases and inaccuracies that are contained in the training data" names bias as a concern, P53.
units.anchor: GAI responses will reflect the biases and inaccuracies that are contained in the training data

units.why: "Be sure to review Harvard's guidelines for use of these tools" points users to the university framework, P56.
units.anchor: Be sure to review Harvard’s guidelines for use of these tools

units.why: "Our challenge is to incentivize the level of engagement that leads to a deeper understanding" gives the learning rationale behind adapting to AI, P41.
units.anchor: incentivize the level of engagement that leads to a deeper understanding

units.why: "We currently don't think twice about use spell-checking and grammar-checking tools" compares AI to everyday tools; no type covers a tool-normalizing analogy (P45 is AI as human collaborator), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: We currently don’t think twice about use spell-checking and grammar-checking tools
units.uncovered_note: Analogy that AI may become as routine as spell-check, calculators and spreadsheets.

documents.title: Teach with Generative AI
documents.stance_why: It says "Schools within Harvard allow for the customization of AI usage policies by individual instructors"; no university-wide rule on student use is set, so the stance is delegation.
documents.summary: A university faculty page promoting teaching with generative AI, with FAQs on using AI for course preparation, redesigning assessments, risks and policies. It leaves student rules to schools and instructors.

units.why: "Schools within Harvard allow for the customization of AI usage policies by individual instructors" delegates the decision to instructors, P04.
units.anchor: customization of AI usage policies by individual instructors
units.frag_start: At the course level, Schools within

units.why: "provided these are clearly communicated" is a condition that instructor policies be communicated, P09.
units.anchor: provided these are clearly communicated
units.frag_start: At the course level, Schools within

units.why: "students and faculty are encouraged to be transparent about the use of generative AI in academic work", with "proper attribution", asks for disclosure of AI use, P24.
units.anchor: students and faculty are encouraged to be transparent about the use of generative AI

units.why: "Consider co-creating course-specific norms around the use of generative AI with your students" lets each course set its own norms: P04.
units.anchor: Consider co-creating course-specific norms around the use of generative AI with your students.

units.why: "ensuring that students' work remains original and reflective of their understanding and skills" states that submitted work be the student's own, P29.
units.anchor: students’ work remains original and reflective of their understanding and skills

units.why: "The use of generative AI must align with the principles of honesty, respect, and responsibility" is a general principle for AI use, P56.
units.anchor: must align with the principles of honesty, respect, and responsibility

units.why: "strike a balance between leveraging these tools for educational enhancement and ensuring that they do not compromise educational objectives" frames the overall principle, P56.
units.anchor: strike a balance between leveraging these tools for educational enhancement

units.why: "Each encourages innovative and thoughtful integration of AI in teaching and learning practices" says Schools encourage integrating AI, P02.
units.anchor: Each encourages innovative and thoughtful integration of AI in teaching and learning practices

units.why: "other existing policies, such as Harvard's Information Security Policy, Digital Accessibility Policy, and Intellectual Property Policy, also apply to GenAI", which sets scope for AI use, P56.
units.anchor: also apply to GenAI and the use of LLMs
units.frag_start: It is also important to remember

units.why: "Personal data is not supposed to be fed to GenAI models" is a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: Personal data is not supposed to be fed to GenAI models.

units.why: "AI models can make mistakes" with "garbled or entirely made-up answers" warns about hallucinations, P31.
units.anchor: yielding garbled or entirely made-up answers

units.why: "AI adopts the biases of the material and data it was trained on" names bias, P53.
units.anchor: AI adopts the biases of the material and data it was trained on.

units.why: "you should shift the kind of assignments you are providing students" tells instructors to redesign assignments because of plagiarism risk, P35.
units.anchor: you should shift the kind of assignments you are providing students

units.why: "enforce academic dhonesty policies" tells instructors to enforce integrity rules for AI misuse, P36.
units.anchor: enforce academic dhonesty policies

units.why: "creating assessments that emphasize skills where AI tools fall short" advises redesigning assessments around AI, P35.
units.anchor: creating assessments that emphasize skills where AI tools fall short

units.why: "Design tasks and assessments that require creativity, practical application of concepts, and critical thinking" is an assessment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Design tasks and assessments that require creativity, practical application of concepts, and critical thinking.

units.why: "test intermediate steps in the learning process, instead of just the final product" shifts grading toward process, P35.
units.anchor: test intermediate steps in the learning process, instead of just the final product

units.why: "at a minimum provide clear guidelines about the use of AI-generated content in assignments and assessments" asks instructors to state AI expectations, P09.
units.anchor: at a minimum provide clear guidelines about the use of AI-generated content

units.why: "AI can help you outline your course, create learning objectives, and suggest assignments" lists instructor uses of AI for course preparation, P59.
units.anchor: outline your course, create learning objectives, and suggest assignments or in-class activities
units.frag_start: Starting a syllabus or a lesson

units.why: "Some faculty have explored how AI tools can help write, modify, or create question sets" describes instructor use for assessment items, P59.
units.anchor: how AI tools can help write, modify, or create question sets

units.why: "LLMs can be used to provide initial personalized feedback to your students" describes instructor feedback use, P59 (not P46, since final grades are not at issue).
units.anchor: LLMs can be used to provide initial personalized feedback to your students

units.why: "Feeding it your syllabus, lectures, and an in-depth prompt can help make a personal tutorbot" suggests a course-specific AI tutor, P17.
units.anchor: Feeding it your syllabus, lectures, and an in-depth prompt can help make a personal tutorbot

units.why: "generate unlimited practice problems" proposes AI-generated practice for students, P14.
units.anchor: generate unlimited practice problems

units.why: "Some of these tools are free and open to all faculty, students and staff behind Harvard Key" says the university provides AI tools, P17.
units.anchor: free and open to all faculty, students and staff behind Harvard Key

units.why: "Harvard has consistently tried to embrace new technology across our classrooms" frames AI as embraced, a default of welcome, P02.
units.anchor: Harvard has consistently tried to embrace new technology across our classrooms

units.why: "GenAI tools have raised concerns about how they may compromise student assessments, promote academic dishonesty, and facilitate lazy learning" gives the learning-risk rationale, P41.
units.anchor: raised concerns about how they may compromise student assessments, promote academic dishonesty

units.why: "it's essential to learn (and perhaps teach) how to write a prompt that works" treats prompting as a skill to teach, P44.
units.anchor: it’s essential to learn (and perhaps teach) how to write a prompt that works

units.why: "AI-tutored students performed as well or better" cites evidence on learning outcomes, P55.
units.anchor: AI-tutored students performed as well or better

units.why: "refer to School-specific policies and resources" sends instructors to school-level policy, P56.
units.anchor: refer to School-specific policies and resources

units.why: "this page will be updated frequently with new resources and advice" says the guidance will change, P54.
units.anchor: this page will be updated frequently with new resources and advice

documents.unit: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Computing in Engineering Education
documents.title: Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The page says the team is "committed to supporting faculty and staff in the effective and responsible integration of Generative AI" and that SEAS is "empowering and encouraging" computational tools; it states no student restriction, so it is welcoming.
documents.summary: A short SEAS service page: the Computing in Engineering Education team supports faculty integrating generative AI into computational courses and links to Harvard integrity guidelines. It sets no student rules.

units.why: "committed to supporting faculty and staff in the effective and responsible integration of Generative AI (G-AI) into SEAS courses" is a unit commitment to support faculty AI integration, P63.
units.anchor: committed to supporting faculty and staff in the effective and responsible integration of Generative AI

units.why: "we recognize the transformative potential of G-AI and believe that it can enhance the computational learning environment" welcomes AI in computational courses, P02.
units.anchor: believe that it can enhance the computational learning environment at SEAS

units.why: "empowering and encouraging using state-of-the-art computational tools and techniques for problem-solving and engineering design" gives the mission rationale for AI, P44.
units.anchor: empowering and encouraging using state-of-the-art computational tools and techniques

units.why: "This includes, but is not limited to, computational-related course activities, lectures, homework assignments, projects, and labs" defines the scope of the AI support, P61.
units.anchor: computational-related course activities, lectures, homework assignments, projects, and labs

units.why: "Interested faculty and staff should contact CEE to request a consultation" offers consultation to faculty learning AI, P63.
units.anchor: Interested faculty and staff should contact CEE to request a consultation.

units.why: "to ensure that students and faculty adhere to Harvard academic integrity standards and best practices" points everyone to the university integrity standards, P56.
units.anchor: ensure that students and faculty adhere to Harvard academic integrity standards and best practices

notes: Coded by Coder B. Provost, HUIT and FAS pages were inaccessible (access denied) and are not coded. SEAS page is thin. Samples repeated in OUE page coded once.
